However, an 8-week program of extremely low-volume HIIT combined with plyometric exercises and iron supplementation had a more beneficial effect compared to traditional iron therapy. These greater improvements in postural control occurred alongside greater improvements in the Hb concentration and muscle endurance in the TG compared to the NTG.

records.title: Effects of a commercially available sugar-free energy drink on hitting exit velocity in experienced baseball and softball players: a randomized crossover trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of a commercially available sugar-free energy drink on hitting exit velocity in experienced baseball and softball players: a randomized crossover trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Caffeine is commonly used as an ergogenic aid, with effective doses often reported at approximately 3-9 mg/kg; however, lower doses are also frequently included in multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements, and the effects of these supplements on sport-specific hitting performance in baseball and softball players remain largely unexplored. Thus, we investigated the acute effects of a commercially available, multi-ingredient caffeinated energy drink (ED) on hitting exit velocity, countermovement jump (CMJ) height, barbell velocity, reaction time, perceived energy, and post-running metabolic outcomes in experienced baseball and softball players.

Methods

Twenty-two experienced baseball and softball players (14 males, 8 females; mean playing experience: 13 ± 2 years) completed this double-blind, randomized, crossover study. Participants consumed either a sugar-free and caffeinated ED (C4 Performance Energy®; 5 kcal, 200 mg caffeine, β-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and vitamin B12) or a low-calorie, flavor-matched placebo (PLA) during two experimental sessions separated by ≥ 5 days. Testing batteries were performed at three within-session timepoints (T0: pre-consumption; T1: 30 minutes post-consumption; T2: post-exercise) and included CMJs, 30 back squat repetitions at 30% of estimated 1RM, a computerized reaction time test, and subjective perceptual questionnaires. Participants also performed 40 tee hits after T1 and before a high-intensity interval treadmill protocol, followed by 15-minute post-exercise indirect calorimetry.

Results

Both average (ED: 71.3 ± 14.0 mph vs. PLA: 70.1 ± 13.5 mph; mean difference ± SD: 1.20  ±  1.41 mph, 95% CI: 0.56-1.84, p < 0.001, dz = 0.85) and peak (ED: 76.7 ± 13.9 mph vs. PLA: 75.1 ± 13.6 mph; mean difference ± SD: 1.56 ± 1.70 mph, 95% CI: 0.79-2.33, p < 0.001, dz = 0.92) hitting exit velocity were significantly greater in the ED condition. A significant condition × time interaction was observed for CMJ height (p = 0.003), whereby jump height was maintained with the ED condition but decreased with PLA at T1. Post-exercise recovery energy expenditure was significantly greater with ED (~5%; p = 0.040, d = 0.46). No significant interactions were observed for barbell velocity, reaction time, or subjective perceptual questionnaires.

Conclusions

Acute consumption of a caffeinated multi-ingredient energy drink resulted in small increases in average and peak hitting exit velocity and attenuated transient decline in CMJ height observed with placebo. These findings warrant future investigations with live-pitching conditions in prolonged game simulation settings.

records.title: Endurance Exercise Training Before Myocardial Infarction Reduces Decline of Myocardial Function in Old Mice.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Endurance Exercise Training Before Myocardial Infarction Reduces Decline of Myocardial Function in Old Mice.
content.abstract:
Background

Pre-infarction endurance training reduces scar formation and adverse cardiac remodeling in rodents; however, evidence is largely restricted to young animals. Whether these benefits extend to aged individuals, the population most affected by myocardial infarction (MI), remains unclear.

Methods

We investigated the effects of 6 weeks of endurance exercise training prior to MI in aged mice (20 months). C57BL/6 mice were randomized to exercise (EX-MI, n=11; treadmill running 30 min/day, 5 days/week) or sedentary conditions (SED-MI, n=12). MI was induced by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending artery. FDG PET imaging was performed on days 5 and 7 post MI, and cardiac structure and function were evaluated by MRI at day 28. Histological analyses were performed ex vivo.

Results

Exercise training resulted in smaller and thicker infarct scars compared with sedentary controls. Despite similar lef t ventricular dilation, EX-MI mice showed significantly improved systolic function, with higher ejection fraction and stroke volume. This was supported by enhanced global longitudinal and radial strain rates. Likewise, regional deformation analysis demonstrated higher circumferential and radial strain within the scar. FDG uptake was increased in the infarct region at day 7. Additionally, remote myocardium was thicker and exhibited greater radial deformation in exercised animals.

Conclusions

Our study shows that short time endurance exercise training in older mice prior to acute MI reduces post-MI left ventricular remodeling, scar size, and scar thinning. Myocardial contractility in both the remote and infarct areas were preserved by endurance training, potentially reflecting an enhanced compensatory capacity induced by pre-infarction exercise training.

records.title: Ischemic Preconditioning Effects in Competitive Swim Athletes: A Randomized Control Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Ischemic Preconditioning Effects in Competitive Swim Athletes: A Randomized Control Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Montgomery, ME, Scholten, HG, and Scholten, SD. Ischemic preconditioning effects in competitive swim athletes: A randomized control trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Ischemic preconditioning (IPC) has been shown to effectively enhance athletic performance in short-duration (250 yard) swimming, possibly through mechanisms related to the vascular system. Swimming is an ideal mode of exercise to test IPC's effectiveness outside of the lab because of the controlled environment. However, it remains unclear whether these benefits persist over longer swimming distances. To address this gap, this study investigated the potential benefits of IPC on performance in a 500-yard swimming event by conducting a block-randomized controlled trial comparing swim times under 2 IPC conditions: a 1-minute sham condition and a 5-minute IPC intervention. Fourteen NCAA Division II swimmers completed all trials. Eleven out of 14 subjects swam faster (1.72 seconds) with IPC treatment than with sham treatment (p = 0.19; effect size = 0.08). This improvement in time is small, but it is worth considering in competitive sports, where the time difference among competitive athletes is small.

records.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Resistance and endurance exercise produce distinct adaptations, but molecular responses that distinguish these exercise modalities across studies and molecular layers remain incompletely defined. We sought to identify reproducible resistance- and endurance-associated molecular responses across human skeletal muscle and plasma omics datasets.

Methods

We integrated publicly available human exercise omics datasets. Random-effects meta-analyses included 15,312 genes from three skeletal muscle RNA-seq datasets and 4,641 proteins from two skeletal muscle proteomic datasets. Early skeletal muscle phosphoproteomic responses were compared across two independent studies using 2,430 matched phosphosites. At 24 hours, skeletal muscle phosphoproteomics and targeted and untargeted metabolomics in skeletal muscle and plasma were analyzed separately; plasma proteomics was not analyzed. Effects were standardized as resistance exercise minus endurance exercise, with significance defined within each molecular layer at FDR<0.05.

Results

RNA-seq identified 269 genes, including 71 resistance-associated and 198 endurance-associated genes. Global proteomics identified 10 proteins (nine resistance-associated; one endurance-associated). Early phosphoproteomic effects correlated across studies (r=0.589, P=4.1x10-227); 210 of 238 significant phosphosites were directionally concordant, and 51 met replication criteria. At 24 hours, targeted plasma metabolomics identified 14 endurance-associated features, while untargeted plasma metabolomics identified 18 features, including nine resistance-associated and nine endurance-associated features. Resistance-associated responses involved contractile, myofibrillar, cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, protein quality-control, stress-response, and phosphorylation-related processes. Endurance-associated responses involved mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, respiratory-chain biology, fatty acid oxidation, substrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial proteostasis.

Conclusions

Human molecular responses to resistance and endurance exercise are molecular-layer specific. Endurance-associated responses were more consistently represented in transcriptomic and metabolic layers, whereas resistance-associated responses were more prominent in protein abundance and phosphorylation. These findings provide a quantitative basis for selecting molecular measurements and sampling strategies in future human resistance and endurance exercise studies.

records.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

records.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
content.abstract:
Background

Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers.

Methods

Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery.

Results

Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences.

Conclusion

Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis.

Clinical trial registration

The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

records.title: Does Increased Maximal Sprint Speed Alter Pacing Distribution in the 400-m Race Among Male 400-m Sprinters? A Longitudinal Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Does Increased Maximal Sprint Speed Alter Pacing Distribution in the 400-m Race Among Male 400-m Sprinters? A Longitudinal Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sato, K, Yoshimoto, T, Chiba, Y, Ohnuma, H, Iso, S, Tsuchiya, J, and Takai, Y. Does increased maximal sprint speed alter pacing distribution in the 400-m race among male 400-m sprinters? A longitudinal study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Performance in the 400-m sprint is influenced not only by short sprint ability but also by pacing strategy during a race. However, the effects of changes in short sprint ability on pacing characteristics remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the effects of changes in maximal sprint speed (MSS) on 400-m sprint performance and segmental running speed in competitive 400-m sprinters. Twenty-three male 400-m sprinters (age: 20.04 ± 1.76 years, height: 1.75 ± 0.06 m, body mass: 66.93 ± 6.93 kg, 400-m personal best: 49.03 ± 1.56 seconds; range: 45.58-52.70 seconds) performed 400-m and 60-m sprint tests on 2 occasions separated by 1 year. Maximal sprint speed was defined as the highest mean running speed among the 10-m segments during a 60-m sprint. In the 400-m sprint, the relative running speed for each 50-m segment (%MSS) was calculated as the mean running speed divided by the MSS, and the percentage of the 400-m time spent in each 50-m segment (%ST) was determined. Sprinters who exhibited greater increases in MSS demonstrated greater improvements in 400-m sprint performance. Furthermore, increases in MSS were significantly associated with improvements in running speed during the 0-250-m segments of the 400-m sprint. These findings indicate that increases in MSS may contribute to improvements in 400-m sprint performance, particularly through enhanced running speed during the first half of the race.

records.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
content.abstract:
Introduction

There is considerable evidence that physical activity can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in muscles, enhance maximal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate, improve physical fitness, and help maintain overall health in humans. On the other hand, there is growing evidence that excessive training load may have a detrimental effect on mitochondria and glucose homeostasis.

Hypothesis

We hypothesized that moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT) would be sufficient to increase muscle mitochondrial oxidative capacity and exercise tolerance in untrained healthy people.

Methods

Eleven young, healthy, untrained males took part in this study. They performed a 7-week endurance training program (MIIT) on a cycle ergometer, composed of 4 sessions per week, each lasting 40 min. Before and after the MIIT training program, a pulmonary maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O 2max ) as well as lactate threshold (LT) were determined and a muscle biopsy from the m. vastus lateralis was taken to evaluate the level of muscle proteins related to energy metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis, and to measure the muscle's maximal mitochondrial respiration rate.

Results

The training resulted in an increase of skeletal muscle homogenate V̇O 2max (by ~50%, P =0.001), due to increased mitochondrial mass and the enrichment of mitochondria with the individual respiratory chain complexes. The MIIT increased the power output at the lactate threshold (PO at LT) by ~43 W ( P =0.001) and the pulmonary V̇O 2max by 7% ( P =0.01) and had no adverse effect on blood glucose homeostasis.

Conclusions

MIIT, which is a less intense form of training than the commonly used types of interval training, effectively induces a range of beneficial muscular and systemic adaptations that contribute to improvement of physical fitness and maintenances good health in humans.

records.title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
content.abstract:
Background

Low energy availability (LEA) adversely affects athletes'physiological health, yet studies in elite synchronized swimmers across different pre-competition training phases are scarce. This study evaluated changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health in Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers before the National Games.

Methods

Ten Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers sequentially completed a 1-week tapering phase (TP) and a 4-week intensified training phase (ITP). At the end of each phase, dietary intake (weighed food records), exercise energy expenditure (heart rate monitoring), energy availability (EA), resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and blood biomarkers were measured. Within each training phase, athletes were classified into LEA and non-LEA groups according to their EA levels, and between-group differences were compared. In addition, overall changes between TP and ITP were analyzed in the full cohort of 10 athletes.

Results

LEA prevalence was 40% during the TP and 60% during the ITP. In unadjusted analyzes, the LEA group showed significantly lower EI (p = 0.025), VO₂ (p = 0.022), mRMR (p = 0.023), RMR ratio (p = 0.006), and intakes of carbohydrate (p = 0.023), protein (p = 0.015), fat (p = 0.032), calcium (p = 0.038), and iron (p = 0.044) during the TP, with large effect-size estimates. As expected from the classification criteria, EA was significantly lower in the LEA group during both the TP (p = 0.001) and ITP (p = 0.005). During the ITP, fat (p = 0.027) and zinc intakes (p = 0.036) were significantly lower in the LEA group, whereas carbohydrate and protein intakes were lower but did not reach statistical significance. In the overall cohort, EEE (p < 0.001) and T4 (p = 0.010) increased from TP to ITP, whereas ferritin (p = 0.012) and calcium intake (p = 0.007) decreased, with large effect-size estimates.

Conclusion

During intensified training, EEE increased without a corresponding increase in EI, suggesting that dietary intake may not have adequately matched the increased training demands and may have increased susceptibility to LEA. LEA was associated with lower energy and macronutrient intakes, potential calcium and iron inadequacies, and phase-specific reductions in RMR-related measures. Phase-related biomarker changes could not be attributed specifically to LEA. Individualized and periodized nutritional monitoring and intervention are recommended to better align energy and nutrient intake with training demands and support athlete health and performance.

records.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
content.abstract:
Abstract

So, YLI, Faricier, R, Guluzade, NA, Belfry, GR, Murias, JM, and Keir, DA. The respiratory compensation point predicts 19.2-km cycling performance in trained male cyclists. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study tested the hypothesis that the step-ramp-step (SRS)-corrected cycling power output (PO) at the respiratory compensation point (RCP) predicts cycling time-trial performance and explored the independent and collective contributions to trial time of 4 physiological variables derived from single or repeated SRS protocols: peak oxygen uptake (V̇o2peak), cycling economy, RCP, and fatigue resistance. Twenty-eight trained male cyclists completed an SRS protocol before and after a 19.2-km virtual time trial (∼30 minutes) on their personal road bikes using a smart trainer. V̇o2peak, cycling economy, and SRS-corrected PO at RCP were derived from the pre-time-trial SRS protocol. Fatigue resistance was quantified as the change in peak ramp PO from pre- to post-time trial. Independent and multilinear regression evaluated the predictive strength of each variable. Relative SRS-corrected RCP (W·kg-1) showed the strongest independent correlation with time-trial completion time (r = -0.61, p < 0.001). Relative V̇o2peak (mL·kg-1·min-1) and cycling economy (%) were also moderately associated with time-trial performance (r = -0.42, p = 0.03; and r = -0.55, p < 0.001, respectively), whereas fatigue resistance was not significantly correlated. In the multilinear regression analysis, SRS-corrected RCP uniquely explained 30.9% of the model's total predictive variance (r = 0.68, p < 0.01) followed by cycling economy (21.3%), ΔPOpeak (2.1%), and absolute V̇o2peak (3.3%). Among trained male cyclists, relative PO at SRS-corrected RCP is a strong and independent predictor of ∼30-minute time-trial performance. The SRS protocol provides a practical, single-session method to assess key physiological determinants of endurance performance, with valuable applications for training prescription and athlete monitoring.

records.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To examine sex-specific lower limb strength, flexibility, and running biomechanics in adolescents with and without OSD.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective chart review of 100 adolescents (n=25 each group): females with OSD (age=14.6 ± 1.9 y; body mass index [BMI]=21.3 ± 2.1 kg/m2); males with OSD (age=14.4 ± 1.6 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2); females without OSD (age=14.8 ± 2.2 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.0 kg/m2); and males without OSD (age=14.4 ± 2.2 y; BMI=22.0 ± 4.6 kg/m2). We assessed mass-normalized sagittal and frontal hip strength and sagittal knee strength via hand-held dynamometry, and quadriceps femoris (prone knee flexion) and hip flexor (Thomas test) flexibility. Limb crossover, contralateral pelvic drop [CPD], medial knee displacement, and tibial dominant stride were assessed during treadmill running. Group differences were analyzed using a two-way multivariate analysis of variance (continuous outcomes) and logistic regression (categorical outcomes), covarying for age and BMI. Analyses were performed using SPSS (alpha set at p<0.05).

Results

Compared with sex-matched healthy peers, females with OSD had impaired hip abduction strength and a greater propensity for CPD and medial knee displacement, though greater hip flexion strength (p≤0.03; Table). Males with OSD had greater hip and knee sagittal plane strength yet impaired flexibility (p≤0.02; Table). Compared with males with OSD, females with OSD had lower hip and knee strength, greater quadriceps femoris flexibility, and higher odds of frontal plane biomechanical deficits (p≤0.02; Table).

Conclusion

We observed sex-specific differences in lower limb muscular and biomechanical features in adolescents with OSD, suggesting that clinicians should consider sex-specific rehabilitation strategies for adolescents with OSD.

records.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Schilling, DT, Abraham, TR, and Elazzazi, A. Should they start or not? A comparative analysis of starter and nonstarter preseason fitness characteristics in NCAA Division III baseball. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Preseason fitness testing in baseball is a widely adopted practice to assess the physical preparedness of players. However, the relationship between these preseason fitness assessments, their ability to differentiate starters from nonstarters in the subsequent season, and their relationship to preseason coaching evaluations is not well-established. This exploratory study aimed to provide a preseason profile of men's NCAA Division III baseball players, compare the differences between starting and nonstarting players, and explore the relationship of these preseason measures to the offensive performance of the starting players at the completion of the season. Starters were considered any hitter who averaged at least 2 plate appearances per team game played or participated in at least 75% of the team's games. Twenty-six players performed 8 preseason fitness tests; and the head coach, blinded to all preseason fitness testing results, subjectively rated the players' batting (power, ball contact, and form) and running performance (speed, agility, and form), resulting in a total offensive performance score (TOPS). In-season offensive performance was measured by each player's on-base plus slugging percentage (OPS). Starters demonstrated significantly greater batted ball velocity, countermovement vertical jump height, unilateral lateral to medial jump distance, medicine ball throw velocity, and faster 60-yard dash and agility T-test times relative to nonstarters. Notably, no significant correlations were observed between any physical performance variable and OPS or TOPS, suggesting that preseason fitness testing may reflect athletic readiness but does not directly relate to offensive performance or coaching evaluation outcomes in this sample.

records.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.

Methods

Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.

Results

Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.

Conclusions

The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

records.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults.

Methods

Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires.

Results

There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments.

Conclusions

A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

records.title: Exploratory observations of sleep during contest preparation in a natural bodybuilder: a case study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory observations of sleep during contest preparation in a natural bodybuilder: a case study.
content.abstract: Natural bodybuilders undergo prolonged caloric restriction combined with high training volumes in the lead-up to competitions to achieve extremely low body fat levels while preserving lean mass. Although sleep plays a critical role in recovery and metabolic regulation, its response to contest preparation remains under-explored. This case study followed a 24-year-old male natural bodybuilder across four months: off-season (AS-1) and a three-month contest preparation phase (AS-2 to AS-5). Body composition, energy status and sleep were assessed. The athlete lost 5.7 kg (6.6%) of initial body mass, including approximately 4.0 kg of estimated fat mass, reaching an estimated body fat percentage of 5.4% two weeks before competition. Energy intake dropped from 4345 to 2080 kcal per day, shifting energy balance from a 1159 kcal surplus at AS-1 to a 1052 kcal deficit at AS-5. Estimated energy availability progressively declined, reaching 23.9 kcal·kg FFM<sup>-1</sup>·day<sup>-1</sup> at AS-5, below a proposed male-specific threshold for potentially low energy availability. Sleep quality deteriorated markedly: sleep efficiency declined from 93% to 83%, wake after sleep onset nearly tripled, and rapid eye movement sleep dropped from 30.8% to 4.4% at AS-4 and 12% at AS-5. Hypnograms showed sleep fragmentation and impaired REM transition. These findings suggest that sleep characteristics may vary during periods of severe energy deficit in bodybuilding contest preparation.

records.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Hammond, KG, Bair, AC, Strang, AJ, Young, JC, Kruskall, LJ, Dunnick, DD, and Schilling, BK. Feasibility of heart rate-based total daily energy expenditure estimation of pararescuemen in garrison. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Pararescuemen are a group of Air Force Special Operations Forces who engage in vigorous daily training to prepare for deployment operations. This training can elicit high-energy expenditure, yet few studies have measured the energy expenditure of these airmen while at their home station (in garrison). Twelve operational pararescuemen (age: 27 ± 3 years; years of service: 5 ± 3 years) were assessed for resting energy expenditure, heart rate (HR) at rest and during initial exercise, and the HR-oxygen consumption (V̇o2) linear equation. Subjects' HR was recorded over 2 normal training days and used to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Subjects reported an average 9 ± 2 hours of sleep per night of analysis and had an average basal metabolic rate = 82 ± 4 kcal·h-1. Average TDEE was 4,021 ± 890 kcals. Pararescuemen expend high levels of energy during routine training at their home station, similar to those of other elite military groups. Observed and reported high-energy expenditures in pararescuemen suggest further investigation into energy intake in this population to optimize performance.

records.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Payne, LKD, Varley, MC, Carey, DL, Driller, MW, and James, LP. Dimensionality reduction of full-body strength-power metrics to identify distinct strength domains in elite rugby union athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to determine the extent of shared and unique information among strength tests and to evaluate whether factors identified through exploratory factor analysis reflect distinct strength domains in professional rugby union players. Twenty professional male rugby union athletes (age 24.4 ± 3.8 years; height 186.3 ± 5.2 cm; body mass 107.6 ± 10.9 kg) completed a battery of 4 upper-body and 5 lower-body isometric, dynamic, and reactive strength tests. A total of 18 metrics were entered into exploratory factor analysis to identify distinct strength domains. Exploratory factor analysis reduced the data set into 2 upper-body domains (pressing and pulling) and 4 lower-body domains (isometric, dynamic, reactive, and relative). These domains together explained 73% of the variance in the upper-body data and 79% of the variance in the lower-body data. The isometric domain was driven by early-phase force at 100 and 200 ms, while peak force contributed less strongly. The dynamic domain was defined by heavy squat velocity, which diverged inversely from countermovement jump height, reflecting load-velocity differences. The reactive domain was shaped by contact time and countermovement depth, highlighting the role of temporal mechanics. The relative domain was defined by drop jump height and countermovement jump momentum, emphasizing the influence of body mass on ballistic force expression. Eighteen test metrics were successfully reduced to 6 distinct domains of strength in professional rugby union athletes. This framework provides a concise basis for profiling upper-body and lower-body strength to reduce redundancy and retain key information needed for training and monitoring rugby athletes.

records.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

records.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Diseases like cardiovascular metabolic disease (CMD) and osteoarthritis (OA) impact health-related quality of life (hr-QoL). In the general population, hr-QoL is associated with physical activity (PA), sedentary time (ST) and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). This study aims to examine 1) associations between device-based and self-reported PA and ST, and hr-QoL, and 2) the influence of self-reported CRF in these associations in people with (or at risk for) CMD and/or OA.

Methods

Data from the Lifestyle front Office For Integrating lifestyle medicine in the Treatment of patients (LOFIT) study was used. Participants included patients with (or at risk for) CMD and/or OA (n=273) within the Netherlands. PA and ST were measured using device-based (activPAL™) and self-reported methods (International Physical Activity Questionnaire - Short Form and Marshall Sitting Questionnaire). CRF was assessed by estimating peak oxygen uptake per kilogram bodyweight (VO2peak mL·kg -1·min -1) using the FitMáx questionnaire. Hr-QoL was assessed using EQ-5D-5L. The associations were examined using linear regression and cross-sectional mediation models.

Results

Higher levels of device-based, and self-reported PA were associated with higher hr-QoL (b=0.007, 95% CI=0.000, 0.013 per 1000 steps, b=0.001 95% CI= 0.000, 0.002 per 30 minutes). Higher levels of device-based and self-reported ST were associated with lower hr-QoL (b=-0.006, 95% CI=-0.012, -0.000 per 30 minutes, b=-0.004, 95% CI=-0.007, -0.001 per 30 minutes). A cross-sectional indirect association via CRF was observed in the association between PA and hr-QoL.

Conclusions

Higher PA and lower ST are associated with enhanced hr-QoL, where CRF influences the relationship between PA and hr-QoL in this patient population. Reducing ST could be a more feasible first step, if increasing PA is challenging. Moreover, the influence of CRF emphasizes the need for interventions focusing on improving fitness levels.

records.title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
content.abstract:
Purpose

This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions.

Methods

Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration.

Results

CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001).

Conclusions

In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.

records.title: Reliability and Minimal Detectable Change of Training Efficiency Index During Preseason and In-Season Training in Professional Rugby League Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Reliability and Minimal Detectable Change of Training Efficiency Index During Preseason and In-Season Training in Professional Rugby League Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Fary, T, Duthie, G, Campbell, P, Jennings, J, Ballard, D, and Johnston, RD. Reliability and minimal detectable change of training efficiency index during preseason and in-season training in professional rugby league athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Training Efficiency Index (TEI) is an integrated method using external and internal loads to monitor responses to the training dose. The aim of this study was to quantify relative and absolute reliability of TEI, comparing daily, weekly, and drill-level TEI measurements. Thirty-nine professional rugby league athletes (26 ± 4 years; 1.86 ± 0.06 m; 97 ± 9 kg) were monitored across the 2025 National Rugby League season. The reliability was assessed in two 4-week blocks during preseason (14 sessions) and in-season (11 sessions). Daily reliability was assessed using 1 prespecified field session per week, weekly reliability was calculated by averaging sessions, and drill-level TEI was calculated from a relatively standardized in-season 13v13 match-simulation training drill. Training Efficiency Index was calculated for each training session using wearable microtechnology, combining 5 different external load variables with Edwards' TRIMP. The reliability was estimated using variance-component linear mixed-effects models with an overall intercept as a fixed effect and athlete as a random intercept. Between-athlete and within-athlete variance were used to derive intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), coefficient of variation, and minimal detectable change (MDC) estimates. Weekly aggregation of TEI was more reliable than daily estimates and more reliable during preseason compared with in-season training. Weekly TEI impulse was most reliable across phases (ICC [95% confidence interval] = 0.86 [0.79-0.89] preseason; 0.79 [0.68, 0.86] in-season), with changes >17% (178.6 TEI impulse units) in preseason and >19% (206.7 TEI impulse units) in-season to exceed the phase-specific MDC. These findings support weekly TEI, particularly TEI impulse, for longitudinal monitoring of training responses in rugby league athletes.

records.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Le Moan, D, Slawinski, J, Lecru, L, Braize, E, Brocherie, F, and Bouten, J. Ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia performed at either 3,000 m or 2,000 m similarly impacts overground performance in under-18 field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to compare the effects of 2 levels of hypoxic stress during ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) on overground repeated-sprint ability (RSA). Fifteen highly trained under-18 male field hockey players performed a 3-week training program with 6 ergocycling-based RSH sessions (3 × 6 10-s "all-out" sprints with 20-second intraset passive recovery and 5-minute interset rest; 2 sessions per week) under moderate (MH, FiO2 14.5%, simulated altitude of 3,000 m, n = 8) or low normobaric hypoxia (LH, FiO2 16.3%, 2,000 m, n = 7). Peak (PPO) and mean power output (MPO) were recorded during each RSH session. At Pre- and Postintervention, overground sprinting horizontal force-velocity profiles and RSA test (6 × 20-m "all-out" sprints interspersed by 20 seconds) were performed. Ergocycling-based PPO (p < 0.001) and MPO (p = 0.015) improved significantly for both groups from training 1 to 6. However, overground theoretical maximal force and theoretical maximal power remained unchanged (both p > 0.377), and theoretical maximal velocity (p = 0.026) was significantly decreased for both groups. Although no significant effect (time, group, interaction) was observed for overground RSA best time and sprint decrement (all p > 0.139), RSA total time decreased (p = 0.048) in both MH and LH (-1.1 ± 2.9% and -0.9 ± 1.0%), indicating performance enhancement, irrespective of the hypoxic stress. Using moderate or low normobaric hypoxic stress during a 3-week ergocycling-based RSH intervention resulted in similar improvement during training, albeit with limited, but not negligible, transferability effect in overground performance.

records.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Villaseca-Vicuña, R, Freitas, TT, Spyrou, K, Marín-Cascales, E, Comyns, T, Loturco, I, and Zabaloy, S. Countermovement jump performance across 10 competitive microcycles in under-18 soccer players: An analysis of delayed and long-term responses to training and official competition. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aims of this study were to (a) determine within-microcycle changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) measures (i.e., jump height, reactive strength index modified [RSImod], and eccentric peak velocity [EPV]) collected 2 days after (MD+2) and 1 day before (MD-1) the match-day across 10 weeks during the competitive period in under-18 soccer players and (b) analyze week-to-week variations in the selected CMJ-metrics collected on MD+2 across the entire mesocycle. Twelve (n = 12) under-18 academy soccer players (age: 17.5 ± 0.5 years; body mass: 71.9 ± 7.7 kg) volunteered to participate in this study. Over 10 competitive weeks, CMJ assessments were recorded on force plates at 2 key microcycle time points: MD+2 (active recovery phase at the start of the microcycle) and MD-1 (end of the microcycle). Results showed significant within-week changes in CMJ height and EPV in most of the training microcycles (p: <0.001 to 0.049) while RSImod showed significant changes in only 4 of the 10 microcycles (p: 0.001 to 0.049). Similarly, the between-week comparisons showed significant variations only in EPV and RSI (p: 0.005 to 0.049). These findings suggest that jump height might be better suited to assess within-week changes, while RSImod appears to hold greater discriminative value for detecting between-week fluctuations. Eccentric peak velocity, in turn, may provide useful information for both within-week and between-week changes in young soccer players.

records.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Wei, X, Zhu, H, Zheng, X, Gao, Y, Huang, J, Chen, X, Vigh-Larsen, JF, Mohr, M, and Krustrup, P. Greater reductions in deceleration compared with sprint ability following repeated high-intensity exercise in male and female soccer players, but no effect on countermovement jump (CMJ) or ball-kicking performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the acute effect of repeated sprint and deceleration on the fatigue of each component (sprint vs. deceleration) and on CMJ and soccer kicking performance, and to investigate the association between deceleration ability and fatigue. Thirty-three high-level male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) college soccer players completed 10 × 15-m sprints with subsequent 5-m enforced deceleration, interspersed with 20-s recovery intervals. Sprint and deceleration performance were measured continuously during the protocol, while CMJ and kicking performance were assessed before and immediately after. Furthermore, the players' deceleration ability was measured using deceleration deficit and deceleration index. Peak deceleration had significantly higher fatigue index (FI) and decrement score (Sdec) compared with speed (p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 3.18-3.32), while no significant decline was found in CMJ or kicking performance after the repeated sprint and deceleration protocol (p > 0.05, Cohen's d = -0.06∼0.23). A significant repeated sprint and deceleration × sex interaction effect was observed in peak ball speed (p < 0.05, ηp2 = 0.149), with women showing a decrease in peak ball speed compared with their male counterparts. The deceleration index correlated with FI and Sdec of speed (r = -0.444∼-0.516, p < 0.05), and the rate of CMJ decline correlated with FI and Sdec deceleration (r = 0.530-0.549, p < 0.05). Finally, the rate of decline in kicking speed was positively correlated with the Sdec deceleration rate (r = 0.423, p < 0.05). Deceleration capacity is more prone to acute fatigue than sprint ability. In addition, repeated sprint and deceleration had a limited effect on athletic performance, but men and women showed different adjusted trends in kicking speed. Finally, players having better deceleration capacity show a smaller performance drop.

records.title: The effect of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep parameters in exercised population: a systematic review and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of randomized controlled trials.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effect of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep parameters in exercised population: a systematic review and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Sleep is crucial for recovery and optimal performance in athletes; however, poor sleep is common during periods of intensive training or competition. The microbiota-gut-brain axis suggests probiotics and synbiotics could modulate sleep, but evidence in exercised populations is limited.

Objective

To systematically review randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep in exercised populations, using a Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) approach.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest were searched up to September 2025. Eligible studies were RCTs including exercised individuals, testing probiotics or synbiotics, and reporting sleep outcomes. Data extraction, risk of bias assessment (RoB 2), and narrative synthesis followed SWiM guidelines.

Results

Six RCTs (n = 180) were included: four probiotic and two synbiotic interventions lasting 4-17 weeks. Populations included athletes from multiple sports across four continents. Nine of twelve primary sleep outcomes favored supplementation, with significant effects for probiotics (combined p < 0.01) and synbiotics (p < 0.001). Benefits were most consistent for subjective sleep quality and, in some cases, sleep latency. Secondary outcomes showed occasional reductions in stress, anxiety, and fatigue.

Conclusion

Probiotic and synbiotic supplementation may improve sleep in exercised populations, especially perceived quality and latency. Evidence supports cautious, adjunctive use, but larger, standardized trials are needed to confirm effects.PROSPERO registration number: CRD420251151264.

records.title: Effects of nutritional interventions on competitive performance and dose‒response relationships among esports players of different skill levels: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of nutritional interventions on competitive performance and dose‒response relationships among esports players of different skill levels: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background and objectives

Esports place exceptional demands on neuropsychological capacities; however, a systematic and quantitative synthesis of the specific efficacy of nutritional interventions across various tasks and competitive populations remains absent. This study aims to evaluate the impact of nutritional supplementation on cognitive function and competitive performance in esports players and to explore key moderating variables.

Methods

Electronic databases, including Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus, were searched (up to January 25, 2026). Thirteen randomized controlled trials (RCTs) met the inclusion criteria. A three-level random-effects model was employed to calculate the pooled effect size (Hedges' g), with sources of heterogeneity explored through subgroup analyses and meta-regression.

Results

Nutritional interventions significantly enhanced esports-related performance (g = 0.92), with the most pronounced benefits observed in processing speed (g = 1.18) and executive function (g = 1.06). Subgroup analyses revealed significant gains in both professional (g = 0.97) and amateur groups (g = 0.92), while the improvement in first-person shooter (FPS) games (g = 0.96) appeared to surpass that in multiplayer online battle athlete (MOBA) games. Meta-regression indicated no significant linear correlation between caffeine dosage and effect size. GRADE assessment categorized the quality of evidence mostly as "low" to "moderate."

Conclusions

Nutritional interventions demonstrate significant potential for optimizing multidimensional cognitive performance in esports players, particularly in enhancing fundamental reaction speed and high-level decision-making processes. While the findings exhibit a degree of robustness, their practical application should be cautiously evaluated within specific competitive contexts due to current limitations in evidence certainty and significant interstudy heterogeneity. Future research characterized by gender balance and mechanistic orientation with long-term intervention protocols is warranted to elevate the level of clinical evidence.

records.title: Effects of serotonergic pharmacological manipulation on exercise performance and central fatigue: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of serotonergic pharmacological manipulation on exercise performance and central fatigue: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Exercise-induced fatigue is a complex, non-pathological state that acutely limits physical performance, and the serotonergic (5-HT) system has been proposed as an important modulator of its central components. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the effects of serotonergic pharmacological manipulation on exercise-related outcomes.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Central, and SportDiscus from inception to August 2025. Randomized controlled trials examining the effects of serotonergic pharmacological manipulation on exercise-related outcomes in healthy adults were included. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using RoB 2.0 were conducted independently. Pooled effects were synthesized using three-level random-effects models, and the certainty and robustness of the evidence were examined in additional analyses.

Results

Twenty-one randomized controlled trials involving 248 healthy adults were included in the systematic review, of which 19 studies involving 229 participants were included in the meta-analysis. In the primary models, serotonergic pharmacological manipulation was associated with small reductions in evoked motor response (Hedges' g = -0.24, 95% CI -0.46 to -0.02), time-domain EMG (Hedges' g = -0.18, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.02), heart rate (Hedges' g = -0.17, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.01), and blood glucose (Hedges' g = -0.50, 95% CI -0.89 to -0.11). Voluntary activation showed a borderline negative pooled estimate (Hedges' g = -0.20, 95% CI -0.40 to 0), whereas ratings of perceived exertion showed a positive but statistically uncertain pooled estimate (Hedges' g = 0.63, 95% CI -0.01 to 1.28). Resting twitch torque showed a small positive pooled effect (Hedges' g = 0.12, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.19), whereas superimposed twitch torque, maximal voluntary contraction, prolactin, lactic acid, and time to task failure did not show clear overall effects.

Conclusions

Overall, this meta-analysis indicates that serotonergic pharmacological manipulation has outcome-specific effects on exercise-related fatigue rather than a single uniform influence across domains. The most consistent primary-model signals were found for evoked motor response, time-domain EMG, heart rate, and blood glucose, whereas overt performance and perceptual outcomes remained more variable. By integrating evidence across different serotonergic interventions and exercise paradigms, these findings improve our understanding of how 5-HT-related mechanisms may contribute to central fatigue during exercise.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
content.abstract: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) has developed an official position on diets for body weight reduction. This critical analysis of the literature is intended to provide a scientific foundation for practitioners, coaches, and trainees regarding the effects of the major diet types in adults who are generally healthy, physically active, and/or athletic, while drawing from clinical research in those with overweight/obesity, when relevant. This position stand does not address acute dehydration-based weight cutting, pharmacotherapy (i.e. GLP-1RAs), or bariatric surgery. The following 15 points constitute the Position Statement of the Society; the Research Committee has approved them. 1) Diets for body weight reduction can be broadly categorized by the magnitude of the energy deficit, linearity of the deficit, and macronutrient composition. These factors need to be tailored to individual preferences, tolerances, and goals.2) Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800-1200  kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, such as calorie-controlled diets. These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, although adequate protein intake and resistance training may mitigate this risk. Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.3) The evidence at-large shows a lack of differential effects between intermittent fasting variants (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating, and twice-weekly fasting) and continuous energy restriction on anthropometric outcomes, although macronutrient quality plays an independent role in optimizing body composition and metabolic health.4) Intra-day meal frequency (as opposed to total daily nutrition) does not tend to crucially influence body weight and body fat reduction. Meal frequency may be individualized flexibly; no lower or upper limits can universally be prescribed to optimize outcomes. However, in physically active and athletic populations, distributing protein across at least three protein-rich meals (or eating occasions) per day may optimize lean mass retention and performance during sustained energy deficits.5) Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.6) For the general population, a daily protein intake of 1.2-1.6 g/kg BW is appropriate for supporting total body weight and fat loss, physical activity, and imparting benefits to musculoskeletal and cardiometabolic health.7) Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6-2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9-3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.8) The dietary carbohydrate‒fat proportion can be individualized to personal preference for the goal of weight loss, since the range of ketogenic to low-fat diets performs similarly.9) Ketogenic diets are effective at bodyweight and body fat reduction, but they also tend to decrease fat-free mass to a greater degree than higher-carbohydrate comparators, particularly in shorter trials where glycogen and total body water shifts can influence estimates.10) Adaptations to weight loss can be physical, physiological, and/or behavioral, and converge toward reducing energy expenditure to fulfill the body's drive toward neutralizing disruptions to homeostasis imposed by the caloric deficit.11) Adaptive thermogenesis is a reduction in resting energy expenditure beyond that predicted by changes in body composition. It can occur in response to hypocaloric conditions and weight loss, but it is not an inevitable response, and it may attenuate substantially upon attainment of weight stability.12) Metabolic adaptations that reduce energy expenditure, including adaptive thermogenesis, and impair gut microbial diversity, can often be attenuated by strategic dietary and exercise programming that foster nutrient-absorption and partitioning, and metabolic flexibility.13) A multitude of tactics can be implemented to manage and overcome plateaus. However, plateaus are also opportunities/cues to practice maintaining progress made thus far (the ultimate goal is the maintenance of a plateau).14) Guidance from an interdisciplinary team of health professionals while maintaining social support is recommended for successful weight management.15) Learning how to prepare home-cooked meals (and plan meals ahead of time through the day) puts dieters in control of their nutritional fate - and in a better position to succeed in managing their body weight and body composition.

records.title: Effects of exercise on metabolic risk, cardiovascular fitness, and body composition in elderly women of the past decade: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of exercise on metabolic risk, cardiovascular fitness, and body composition in elderly women of the past decade: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Age-related reductions in physical activity and unfavorable body composition changes promote metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular risk elevation in older populations. Due to estrogen-related factors, differences in cardiovascular risks, and musculoskeletal conditions, exercise may be one of the most accessible and widely applicable lifestyle interventions for older women. A comprehensive and systematic search has not yet been carried out on the effects of exercise on cardiovascular risk and its related indicators in elderly women. This meta-analysis evaluates exercise effects on metabolic risk, cardiovascular health, and body composition in healthy elderly women.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, and Sinomed (2014-2024) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing supervised exercise with nonexercise controls. Data were analyzed with fixed- and random-effect models in Stata 17.0. The Cochrane RoB2 tool assessed bias risk, while the certainty of evidence was evaluated through the GRADE approach.

Results

Twenty-three RCTs (33 intervention arms, 23 controls) were included. Exercise significantly reduced triglycerides (TG) (-8.56 mg/dL, 95% CI: -16.72, -0.40), total cholesterol (TC)(-26.67 mg/dL, 95% CI: -34.92, -18.42), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) (-23.77 mg/dL, 95% CI: -34.48, -13.05), blood glucose (Glu) (-5.59 mg/dL, 95% CI: -10.12, -1.06), and C-reactive protein (CRP) (-0.86 mg/L, 95% CI: -1.37, -0.35). Cardiovascular improvements included increased VO2peak (+2.78 mL/kg/min, 95% CI: 1.87, 3.70) and reduced systolic blood pressure (SBP) (-8.35 mmHg) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) (-3.26 mmHg). Regarding body composition, relative body fat (RF, i.e. body fat percentage) decreased (-2.47%, 95% CI: -3.42, -1.53), but no significant changes were observed in body weight, trunk fat mass (TFM), waist circumference (WC), fat-free mass (FFM), or skeletal muscle mass (SMM). According to the GRADE framework, the evidence was of moderate certainty for reductions in TC, TG, RF, VO₂peak, and SBP; and low certainty for all other outcomes.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis provides evidence that appropriate exercise (aerobic, resistance, combined exercise) effectively reduces cardiovascular risk factors in elderly women via dual mechanisms of body composition remodeling and metabolic homeostasis enhancement, with particular efficacy in lipid regulation and blood pressure control.

records.title: The effectiveness of protein supplements on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery - a Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effectiveness of protein supplements on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery - a Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Protein supplements are a popular category of dietary supplements among fitness enthusiasts and athletes. However, research providing definitive conclusions on the effects of protein on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery remains limited. Key factors, such as protein source, timing, and optimal dosage, require further investigation to clarify their impact.

Method

A systematic search across seven databases identified 6,129 studies, which were screened using the Covidence online tool. After independent selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment by two reviewers, 75 studies involving 1,206 athletes were included in the meta-analysis. A multilevel meta-analysis synthesized data from the included studies using a Bayesian hierarchical model with the brms package. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot generated with the PublicationBias package and by calculating the P value of Egger's test through the metafor package. Additionally, a moderation analysis with the brms package was conducted to examine the relationship between seven moderators and effect sizes.

Results

The results demonstrated that the effects of protein-carbohydrate supplements showed statistical significance in comparison to the placebo group [μ(SMD): 0.57, 95% CI: 0.2 to 0.93] in enhancing endurance performance. Pure protein supplements demonstrated statistically significant effects compared to the placebo group in both endurance performance [μ(SMD): 0.37, 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.71] and muscle strength [μ(SMD): 0.72, 95% CI: 0.18 to 1.27]. For post-exercise recovery, pure protein supplements also showed statistically significant effects compared to carbohydrate supplements for maintaining glycogen resynthesis [μ(SMD): 0.83, 95% CI: 0.21 to 1.46]. However, the results indicated that all significant effects were observed in randomized controlled trials where the energy intake between the intervention and control groups was not matched.

Conclusion

The effects of protein supplementation on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery appear to be limited. Protein supplements showed beneficial effects compared to no supplementation. However, all statistically significant results were derived from studies in which energy intake was not matched between groups. This suggests that the observed benefits may not be attributable to protein per se. An additional intake of 1 g/kg/day of protein from supplements, resulting in a total daily protein intake of approximately 2 g/kg/day, appears to be most effective for enhancing athletic performance.

Registration

Registered at the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (identification code CRD42024608194).

records.title: Does sedentary behaviour cause spinal pain in children and adolescents? A systematic review with meta-analysis.

content.title: Does sedentary behaviour cause spinal pain in children and adolescents? A systematic review with meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate whether sedentary behaviour is a risk or prognostic factor for spinal pain in children and adolescents. Specifically, to estimate the (1) direction and strength of the association; (2) risk of spinal pain onset and (3) effect on spinal pain prognosis.

Design

Systematic review with meta-analysis.

Data sources

Electronic searches of MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and Web of Science up to 23 March 2023.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Reports estimating the effect of sedentary behaviour on spinal pain in young people (≤19 years).

Results

We included 129 reports, 14 were longitudinal (n = 8 433) and 115 were cross-sectional (n > 697 590). We incorporated 86 studies into meta-analyses. (1) From cross-sectional data, we found low certainty evidence of a small positive association between sedentary behaviour and spinal pain (adjusted odds ratio 1.25 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.33), k = 44, n > 92 617). (2) From longitudinal data, we found low certainty evidence of no increased risk for the onset of spinal pain due to sedentary behaviour (adjusted risk ratio 1.07 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.35), k = 4, n = 1 292). (3) No studies assessed prognosis.

Conclusion

Cross-sectional data suggest minimally higher odds of spinal pain for children and adolescents who engage in greater sedentary behaviours. However, longitudinal data do not support a causal relationship, indicating that sedentary behaviour does not increase the risk for onset of spinal pain. Due to the low certainty of evidence, these findings must be interpreted with caution. We found no evidence of the effect sedentary behaviour has on spinal pain prognosis in children and adolescents, highlighting a considerable gap in the literature.

records.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
content.abstract:
Purpose
